content: Lichen planus is a condition characterized by an itchy rash that can appear on the skin or inside the mouth. Symptoms of Lichen Planus: Mouth Lesions: Lesions in the mouth may be tender or painful, although mild cases might not cause any discomfort. These lesions are commonly found on the sides of the tongue or the inner cheeks, and sometimes on the gums. They may appear as blue-white spots or small pimples. The lesions often form a lacy, net-like pattern. Over time, the affected area may gradually increase in size. In some cases, the lesions can develop into painful ulcers. Skin Lesions: Skin lesions are typically located on the inner wrists, legs, torso, or genital areas. They are often itchy and appear symmetrically on both sides of the body. Lesions may occur as single papules or clusters, frequently at sites of previous skin injury. Papules are usually 2–4 cm in size and may cluster together to form larger, flat-topped lesions. The lesions have distinct, sharp borders and may be covered with fine white streaks or scratch marks, known as Wickham's striae. They can have a shiny or scaly appearance and are often dark-colored, ranging from reddish-purple (on the skin) to gray-white (in the mouth). In some cases, blisters or ulcers may develop. Other Symptoms: Dry mouth. Hair loss. A metallic taste in the mouth. Nail abnormalities, such as ridges in the nails. Causes of Lichen Planus: The exact cause of lichen planus is unknown, but it is believed to be related to an allergic or immune reaction. It most commonly affects middle-aged adults and is less frequent in children. Risk Factors: Exposure to certain medications, dyes, and chemicals, including gold, antibiotics, arsenic, iodides, chloroquine, quinacrine, quinidine, phenothiazines, and diuretics. Underlying disorders such as hepatitis C. When to Seek Medical Attention: Contact your healthcare provider if your symptoms persist. Seek care if the appearance of the skin or mouth lesions changes. If the condition continues or worsens despite treatment, consult a medical professional. If your dentist suggests adjusting medications or treating conditions that may trigger the disorder, follow their advice. Diagnosis: Diagnosis is often based on the appearance of the skin or mouth lesions. A biopsy of a skin or mouth lesion can confirm the diagnosis. Blood tests may be performed to rule out hepatitis. Treatment Options: The primary goal of treatment is to alleviate symptoms and promote healing of the lesions. Mild cases may not require treatment. Treatment options include: Antihistamines to reduce itching. Immunosuppressant medications, such as cyclosporine, for severe cases. Lidocaine mouthwashes to numb the area and make eating more comfortable (for mouth lesions). Topical corticosteroids (e.g., clobetasol) or oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) to reduce swelling and suppress immune responses. Corticosteroids may also be injected directly into a lesion. Topical retinoic acid cream (a form of vitamin A) and other ointments or creams to reduce itching, swelling, and aid healing. Topical immune-suppressing medications, such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, though these require careful monitoring for signs of cancer. Dressings may be applied over topical medications to protect the skin from scratching. Ultraviolet light therapy may be beneficial in some cases. Oral retinoids, such as acitretin. Prognosis: Lichen planus is generally not harmful and often improves with treatment. The condition typically resolves within 18 months but may last for weeks to months and can recur over several years. If caused by a medication, the rash should subside once the medication is discontinued. Possible Complications: Long-standing mouth ulcers may increase the risk of developing oral cancer.
